01-01.quote: Seven hundred times a second. That's how often one rapper's catalog gets played on Spotify, and by the time the day closes out it comes to fifty-nine million.

02-02a.quote: Curren$y was on the 2009 XXL Freshman cover

02-02b.quote: and every song he has ever put on the platform — the mixtapes, the Jet Life run, the features, all of it stacked end to end — adds up to what this one catalog moves in twenty-four days.

03-03.quote: Ninety-three rappers, one dot each. Higher dot, more plays per day. Start at the bottom.

04-04.quote: Near the top, Future. Travis Scott. Then one dot with open air under it. More than both of them added together.

05-05a.quote: A catalog pulling that much every day, in 2026, sitting on top of everybody.

05-05b.quote: What year of his career is this? Pick a number.

06-06.quote: So Far Gone came out in 2009. This chart covers the year that ends on its seventeenth anniversary.
06-06.note: 4 was selected as a add on because its the only one that can represent "This chart covers the year that ends on its seventeenth anniversary"

07-07.quote: Year seventeen of a rap career is anniversary-tour territory. Deluxe reissues with three unreleased demos on the back. A festival slot at seven-forty, before the headliner.

08-08.quote: The explanations write themselves. Big back catalog. Half of it is other people's songs. Seventeen years to pile it up.

09-09.quote: Latto's biggest is half of everything she's ever streamed. Jay Rock's is fifty-two percent. Ab-Soul's, seventy-one. Biz Markie, seventy-nine.

10-10.quote: You've got the shape now. Call it. What share of Drake's streams is his single biggest song?

11-11a.quote: Three percent. His ten biggest songs together come to fifteen percent.

11-11b.quote: The next-flattest catalog at anything close to this size is Future, at twenty-four.
11-11b.note: should've offered on of the spatial scenes. this is comparing 2 entities output

12-12a.quote: Ab-Soul falls twenty-eight places. Latto falls thirteen. Jay Rock, twelve.

12-12b.quote: Macklemore keeps seventy-three percent of his streams and drops three spots. Drake loses four point four billion streams, keeps ninety-seven percent of his total, and finishes exactly where he started.

13-13a.quote: He has thirty songs past a billion streams. Thirty-five of the ninety-three rappers on the opening chart have zero.

13-13b.quote: And eighty-one of the ninety-three don't have thirty billion streams across everything they've ever recorded.

14-14.quote: Take his ten biggest. Then take the single biggest song from each of the next five artists and add those five together. His ten win, twenty-one billion to fifteen.

15-15.quote: In 2010, XXL offered him a spot on the Freshman cover. He turned it down.
15-15.note: 1 or 2 plus b-roll since we have footage

16-16.quote: The rappers on that cover, and on the one the year before, came up on the same clock he did. 2009: Kid Cudi, B.o.B, Wale, Curren$y. 2010: J. Cole, Nicki Minaj, Wiz Khalifa, Big Sean, Nipsey Hussle, Jay Rock, Freddie Gibbs.
16-16.note: equal-sized scrolling grid, should be a different document/screen template

17-17.quote: One rule, applied to everybody. A record you lead, or share the lead on equally, counts in full. A feature or a remix verse counts at half.

18-18.quote: That's the 2010 class under the rule. Nicki at thirty billion. Cole at twenty-nine. Stack all seven end to end. Ninety-seven billion. Seven careers.
18-18.note: not enough options, beat is almost asking for 3 things, 1 at each sentence

19-19.quote: Ninety-six and a half billion. His own records, nothing else, are the whole class. Seven rappers with everything they have ever made against one man with only the songs that carry his name first, and it comes down to a coin flip.

20-20.quote: That's the class. Now put the same slice against the names near the top of the opening chart, full catalogs, everything at full credit. Travis Scott, sixty-seven billion. Kendrick, fifty-seven. Post Malone, fifty-six. Future, fifty-four. The slice clears every one of them.

21-21a.quote: He gets accused of living on features. He's done a hundred and eighty-one of them. Future has done two hundred thirty-two. Young Thug, three hundred and two.

21-21b.quote: Fewer verses than either, more streams than anyone: forty-three billion, roughly two hundred forty million a verse.
21-21b.note: there's a template from 3dz-charts--scene-003 that would've been perfect. put them in a ui grid, I'll show you

22-22.quote: There's one place the comparison turns on him. Add the 2009 class to the 2010 class, eleven rappers under the rule, and together they edge him by about three percent. Eleven careers to one, and it's close.

23-23.quote: A song from 2015 streams in 2026 without the artist lifting a finger. Music has no body that gives out. So the top of the daily chart in year seventeen could be a very large archive on autoplay while the man himself stopped mattering somewhere around Views.

24-24.quote: If he'd gone quiet there's one place it shows up first. New records either chart or they don't. Seventeen years since So Far Gone. Pick the year the ticks stop lighting.
24-24.note: b-roll and/or the timeline template clips. they absolutely should've been in here

25-25a.quote: They don't stop. Eighteen straight years with something on a US chart,

25-25b.quote: and one other rapper in the set has that streak — J. Cole, off the cover he turned down.

26-26.quote: Number one as a lead single. Eleven times. Number one as an album. Nine. Number one as somebody else's guest. Four. Number one as a mixtape. Three. Number one as a joint album. Two. Number one as a compilation. One.

27-27.quote: The ones who carry their own records — Post Malone, forty-nine billion on his own songs against six as a guest. XXXTentacion, thirty-five and six. Kendrick, forty-one and sixteen. And the ones who live on other people's hooks. Ty Dolla $ign, five billion on his own records and twenty-two as a guest. Young Thug, eleven and twenty-one. 21 Savage, sixteen and twenty-three.

28-28.quote: Two floors, fixed before the names go in. Thirty billion on your own records. Twenty billion on everyone else's. Five clear the left floor. Seven clear the right. Panels come together and two names are standing in the middle. Drake. And Travis Scott.

29-29a.quote: Lil Baby is certifying his own records at a faster yearly clip than Drake has averaged across the whole run — about twenty-two million units a year against twenty and a half.
29-29a.note:
Fixed-scale small-field outlier
Layout: T2 · Three-Point Outlier would've been perfect or the one I mentioned earlier from this family: 3dz-charts--scene-002

29-29b.quote: Kendrick, Post Malone and Travis Scott have each put five lead singles at number one.

29-29c.quote: Best rapper alive is an argument, and this chart can't referee it. It counts plays. That's the whole job.

30-30a.quote: And the rappers this should really be measured against — the ones whose seventeenth year happened before streaming counted anything — can't go on this chart at all. There's no daily meter for Jay-Z's year seventeen.

30-30b.quote: So *unprecedented* only reaches back as far as the streaming era, and that's as far as I'm taking it.
